The years went the way the tides went, in and out and in.

The log grew thick. Maren's hand changed in it, firmer and then looser, and the ink changed when the shop stopped stocking the old kind. The lines said the same thing. Wound. Ten past. Sometimes the wind. Sometimes nothing.

Erris Kessock grew up and did not leave. There were boats enough now to keep a girl, and then a woman, in Skerrin. She still sat on the wall outside the harbour office most evenings, though she had long since stopped swinging her heels.

"What time is it?" she said.

"Ten to twelve."

"You'll be going up, then."

It was a thing they said. Neither of them thought about it.

The night Maren's knee gave on the eleventh step, she stood a while with her hand on the cold rail and listened to the clock above her, and to the water below, and did not count. Then she went on up.

Erris was in the lamp-room. Maren had not heard her on the stair. She was standing by the window with her back to the harbour and her hands in her coat, and she did not say how she had got there or why, and Maren did not ask.

Maren took off the left glove. She took the key from her pocket. It was warm. She held it out, and Erris took it, and set it in by touch.

They waited for the minute hand.

At ten past, three turns. Then the door, and the stair, and the long dark down."
